title: Identifying and characterizing superspreaders of low-credibility content on Twitter
screen_reason: Behavioural Twitter data (Decahose 10% sample, Jan-Oct 2020; 2,397,388 tweets linking to 738 Iffy+ low-credibility sources, by 448,103 users). A network-dismantling analysis reports a top group of accounts expressed as a % of accounts together with their share of all retweets of low-credibility content: top 10 accounts (0.003% of accounts) account for 34.6% and the top 1,000 (0.25%) for 73-78%. That is CONCENTRATION with both conc_group_pct and conc_share_pct stated (R1 satisfied).

estimates.country: Not stated (Twitter Decahose global 10% sample; Iffy+ list of predominantly US/English-language low-credibility sources)
estimates.date: Observation period Jan-Feb 2020; evaluation period Mar-Oct 2020 (collection Jan 2020-Oct 2020)
estimates.measure_type: share of all retweets of low-credibility content in the following eight months attributable to the top 10 superspreader accounts (0.003% of active accounts), h-index ranking
estimates.value_raw: removing the top 10 superspreaders eliminates 34.6% and 34.3% of the low-credibility content based on h-index and Influence, respectively (optimal: 38.1%); 0.003% of the accounts active during the evaluation period ... received over 34% of all retweets of this content
estimates.conc_group_label: top 10 superspreader accounts by h-index (accounts consistently originating retweeted posts linking to low-credibility sources), identified in Jan-Feb 2020 and evaluated Mar-Oct 2020
estimates.denominator: all retweets of posts linking to low-credibility sources in the Mar-Oct 2020 evaluation retweet network (~394,000 users; total edge weight of the evaluation network); the group denominator is the accounts active during the evaluation period, of which the top 10 are 0.003%
estimates.definition: an account's share is the proportion of low-credibility retweet volume removed from the evaluation network when the account and all retweets of its low-credibility posts are deleted (M_i, Eq 1)
estimates.misinfo_def: "we rely on the Iffy+ list [38] of 738 low-credibility sources compiled by professional fact-checkers"; the paper notes "some individual articles from a low-credibility source might be accurate, and some individual articles from a high-credibility source might be inaccurate"
estimates.n: ~394,000 accounts in the Mar-Oct 2020 evaluation retweet network; 47,012 accounts posted low-credibility links in the observation period
estimates.source_quote: In fact, removing the top 10 superspreaders eliminates 34.6% and 34.3% of the low-credibility content based on h-index and Influence, respectively (optimal: 38.1%). In other words, 0.003% of the accounts active during the evaluation period posted low-credibility content that received over 34% of all retweets of this content over the eight months following their identification.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Iffy+ list of 738 low-credibility source domains compiled by professional fact-checkers (Media Bias/Fact Check-derived); applied automatically to links in tweets. No per-article verification; the authors state the limitation explicitly.
estimates.moderator_quote: Tweets are gathered from a historical collection based on Twitter's Decahose Application Programming Interface (API) [40]. The Decahose provides a 10% sample of all public tweets. ... From this sample, we extract all tweets that link to at least one source in our list of low-credibility sources. This process returns a total of 2,397,388 tweets sent by 448,103 unique users.
estimates.notes: value_pct uses the h-index ranking (34.6%); the Influence ranking gives 34.3% and the oracle/optimal upper bound 38.1% - these are alternative rankings of the same top-10 group, not separate estimates, so one row is kept. conc_dimension=sharing because the share denominator is retweets of low-credibility posts (diffusion volume), not exposure. within_misinfo_content=true in the sense that the whole denominator is low-credibility content (the study never reports low-credibility content as a share of all Twitter content), which is inherent to a CONCENTRATION row. The group percentage (0.003%) is computed by the authors against accounts active in the evaluation period, while the top-10 accounts were selected in the observation period - a slight denominator mismatch the paper itself introduces. Caveat for pooling: 'approximately 13% of the low-credibility retweets in the evaluation network are by accounts who did not create low-credibility posts during the observation period', so the dismantling curves cannot reach 0%.

estimates.moderator_quote: We create four separate rankings of the 47,012 users that created at least one post linking to low-credibility content during the observation period based on each of the metrics defined above: h-index, Popularity, Influence, and Bot Score.
estimates.notes: Kept as range_not_point because the paper reports the interval 73-78% spanning the h-index and Influence rankings without attributing a single figure to either; the optimal (oracle) upper bound is 81%. Reported alongside the top-10 row because the two group sizes are the paper's two headline concentration statements, not sub-rows of one another. The source quote preserves the PDF's end-of-line hyphenation ('elimi- nates', 'con- centration').

missed_or_uncertain: (1) No prevalence share is extractable: the corpus is by construction only tweets that link to low-credibility sources (2,397,388 tweets, 448,103 users), and the paper never reports these as a share of all Decahose tweets, so there is no CONTENT/SHARING denominator. (2) The abstract's 0.1% of users / 80% of misinformation figure (2016 US election) is cited FROM another study [6] and is therefore excluded by R8. (3) Descriptive statistics of the superspreader sample were not extracted because they characterise accounts inside a misinformation-only set rather than the prevalence of misinformation: of the top 1% of accounts with h-index above zero (181 accounts) plus 181 Influence-ranked accounts, 128 (55.1%) were inactive at analysis time and 111 of those (86.7%) suspended; of the 104 still-active accounts, 52% (54) were political, 13.4% (14) 'other', 18.3% (19) media outlets and affiliated personal accounts; 91% (49 of 54) of political superspreaders and 91% (63 of 69) of politically classifiable accounts were conservative; 3% of suspended accounts were verified; manual classification agreed on 211 of 250 accounts (84.4%, Krippendorff's alpha = 0.79). (4) Fig 3/Fig 4 report medians of the proportion of shared sources that are low-credibility for superspreaders vs typical users; the text gives effect sizes and P-values but I could not read a verbatim percentage value out of the figure text, so no row was written for it - an adjudicator with the figure may find a usable median proportion there. (5) 'approximately 13% of the low-credibility retweets in the evaluation network are by accounts who did not create low-credibility posts during the observation period' is a property of the dismantling design, not a prevalence or concentration estimate.

rob.design: Twitter Decahose (10% random sample of all public tweets), Jan-Oct 2020; all tweets linking to any of 738 Iffy+ low-credibility domains extracted (2,397,388 tweets, 448,103 users). Observation window Jan-Feb 2020 (131k users in the retweet network; 47,012 accounts posted at least one low-credibility link) used to rank accounts by h-index, Popularity, Influence and BotometerLite bot score; evaluation window Mar-Oct 2020 (394k users) used to measure each account's share of low-credibility retweet volume via network dismantling, benchmarked against an oracle optimal ranking. Statistical comparison by Cramer-von Mises two-sample tests with 5,000-resample bootstrap CIs. Manual account classification into 16 categories by multiple coders: agreement on 211 of 250 accounts (84.4%), Krippendorff's alpha = 0.79, remainder adjudicated. Main limitations: source-level (not article-level) credibility labels; a 10% sample; retweets only (quote tweets excluded); no country stratification.
rob.item6_quote: To identify this content, we rely on the Iffy+ list [38] of 738 low-credibility sources compiled by professional fact-checkers-an approach widely adopted in the literature [2, 6, 12, 35, 39]. This approach is scalable, but has the limitation that some individual articles from a low-credibility source might be accurate, and some individual articles from a high-credibility source might be inaccurate.
rob.item10_quote: In fact, removing the top 10 superspreaders eliminates 34.6% and 34.3% of the low-credibility content based on h-index and Influence, respectively (optimal: 38.1%). ... Removing the top 1,000 superspreaders (0.25% of the accounts who posted during the evaluation period) eliminates 73-78% of the low-credibility content (optimal: 81%).
